front: What is a finite probability space?
back: A finite set Omega of outcomes with weights p(omega) > 0 that sum to 1. The probability of an event A is the sum of the weights of its outcomes (Section 1).

front: What is a random variable on a finite probability space?
back: A function X from Omega to the real numbers (Definition 1.1). The weights belong to the probability space, not to X.

front: What is the distribution of a random variable X?
back: The map x to P(X = x), the sum of p(omega) over the outcomes with X(omega) = x (Definition 1.2). Its support is the set of values X takes, and a value is in the support exactly when P(X = x) > 0.

front: What is the distribution function of X?
back: F(x) = P(X <= x) for real x (Definition 2.1).

front: What is the shape of the distribution function of a finite law?
back: Hypotheses: positive weights and distinct values x_1, x_2 through x_m, in increasing order. Then F(x) = 0 for x < x_1 and F(x) = 1 for x >= x_m; F is nondecreasing and equals F_k = p_1 + p_2 through p_k on [x_k, x_(k+1)); and F_m = 1 (Proposition 2.2 (a)-(c)).

front: Does the distribution function of a finite law jump at each value, and by how much?
back: Yes. F is right-continuous, and at each value x_k it jumps by p_k > 0, so F(x_k) minus the left limit at x_k equals p_k (Proposition 2.2(d)).

front: What is the quantile function of X?
back: For 0 < p <= 1, Q(p) = inf{x in R : F(x) >= p} (Definition 3.1). This left-endpoint convention is the one used throughout M4. Other conventions give different values at jump points.

front: What is Q(p) for a finite law with distinct values x_1, x_2 through x_m in increasing order?
back: Hypotheses: positive weights, distinct values, 0 < p <= 1. Q(p) = x_(k*), where k* is the least index k with F_k >= p. The index exists because F_m = 1 >= p (Proposition 3.2).

front: What does Remark 3.3 say about the jumps of Q?
back: With F_0 = 0: for 1 <= k <= m and F_(k-1) < p <= F_k, Q(p) = x_k. In particular Q(F_k) = x_k, and Q is left-continuous on (0, 1].

front: What is the quantile of n equally likely distinct values?
back: Hypotheses: distinct y_1 < y_2 through y_n, each with probability 1/n, and 0 < p <= 1. Then Q(p) = y_(ceil(pn)), the ceil(pn)-th smallest value, where ceil(pn) is the least integer at least pn (Proposition 3.4).

front: Which index is the 99% quantile of 150 equally likely distinct losses?
back: 149. Here pn = 148.5 and its ceiling is 149; the floor, 148, is the wrong index (Example 3.5).

front: For the table of Example 3.6, what are Q(1/2), Q(3/5) and Q(61/100)?
back: 0, 0 and 1. The table takes -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3 with F values 1/10, 3/10, 3/5, 4/5, 9/10, 1 (Example 3.6).

front: Is F(Q(p)) = p always true?
back: No. Proposition 3.2 gives F(Q(p)) >= p. In Example 3.6, Q(1/2) = 0, but F(0) = 3/5, not 1/2.

front: If p = F(x_k), does Q(p) move up to x_(k+1)?
back: No. Remark 3.3 gives Q(F_k) = x_k, because the condition F(x) >= p includes equality. In Example 3.6, Q(3/5) = 0. Q moves to 1 only for p above 3/5.

front: Is the 99th percentile of 150 values the 148th smallest, because 148.5 is taken down?
back: No. The index is the least integer at least pn, so Proposition 3.4 gives ceil(148.5) = 149.

front: Does the grid check of Lab 1 prove Proposition 3.2 for every p?
back: No. Lab 1 compares the two forms of Q at 100 grid points p = j/100 for one table. The proof of Proposition 3.2 covers every p in (0, 1].

front: What is the expectation of a random variable with distinct values x_1, x_2 through x_m?
back: E[X] = sum over k of x_k p_k, where p_k = P(X = x_k) (Definition 1.1). It is a probability-weighted average and need not be one of the values.

front: Does summing X(omega) p(omega) over outcomes give the same expectation?
back: Yes. The sum over outcomes equals the sum over values of x_k p_k (Proposition 1.2), because the events {X = x_k} partition the outcome set.

front: Is expectation linear on a finite probability space?
back: Yes. For random variables U and V on the same space and constants alpha, beta, gamma, E[alpha U + beta V + gamma] = alpha E[U] + beta E[V] + gamma (Proposition 1.3).

front: How is the expectation of a law with a density f defined?
back: E[X] = integral of x f(x) dx over the real line, whenever the integral of |x| f(x) dx is finite (Definition 1.6). The integral over the whole line is the limit of definite integrals as the endpoints go to plus or minus infinity.

front: What are the variance and the standard deviation of X?
back: Var(X) = E[(X - mu)^2] with mu = E[X], and the standard deviation is the square root of Var(X) (Definition 2.1). A variance is never negative, because it is the expectation of a square.

front: What is the shortcut formula for variance?
back: Hypotheses: finite probability space with positive weights. Var(X) = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2 (Proposition 2.2).

front: How does variance change under X to aX + b?
back: Var(aX + b) = a^2 Var(X) for constants a and b (Proposition 2.3). The shift b does not change the variance.

front: When is the variance of a finite law zero?
back: Hypotheses: finite probability space with positive weights. Var(X) = 0 if and only if X takes exactly one value (Proposition 2.4).

front: What are E[X] and Var(X) for a fair six-sided die?
back: E[X] = 7/2 and E[X^2] = 91/6, so Var(X) = 35/12 (Examples 1.4 and 2.5).

front: What are the mean and variance of the two-point loss of Example 1.5, in cents?
back: E[L] = 12500 cents and Var(L) = 2968750000 cents squared. The standard deviation is about 54486.24 cents (Example 2.6).

front: Is the expectation always one of the values the variable takes?
back: No. For a fair die E[X] = 7/2, which is not a face of the die (Example 1.4).

front: Does scaling X by a multiply its variance by a?
back: No. Var(aX) = a^2 Var(X) (Proposition 2.3). For the die with a = 2 the variance is 35/3, which is 4 times 35/12, not twice.

front: Is the variance the expectation of X^2?
back: No. Var(X) = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2 (Proposition 2.2). For the die E[X^2] = 91/6, about 15.17, while Var(X) = 35/12, about 2.92.

front: Does a seeded sample mean equal the expectation?
back: No. Lab 2 prints a die sample mean of 3.469 for seed 2026, against E[X] = 7/2. A sample mean is an estimate from one run.

front: Does Var(2X) equal 4 Var(X) for the die?
back: Yes. Var(2X) = 35/3, which is 4 times 35/12 (Lab 2 prints True for this check; Proposition 2.3).

front: For a finitely valued X, is E[(X - c)^2] smallest at c = E[X]?
back: Yes. For every real c, E[(X - c)^2] = Var(X) + (E[X] - c)^2 (Problem P2), so the minimum is at c = E[X].

front: How many losses does the seed-2027 run of Lab 2 print in 10000 draws?
back: 489, against an expected count of 500. The lab prints one run and does not give the spread of the count.

front: What are the k-th moment and the k-th central moment of X?
back: The k-th moment is E[X^k]. The k-th central moment is m_k = E[(X - mu)^k], with mu = E[X] (Section 1).

front: What are the first two central moments?
back: m_1 = 0 and m_2 = Var(X) (Proposition 1.1).

front: What is the standardized variable Z of X?
back: Z = (X - mu)/sigma with sigma = sqrt(Var(X)) > 0. This needs X to take at least two values. Z has mean 0 and variance 1 (Definition 2.1; Proposition 2.2).

front: What are skewness and kurtosis?
back: Skewness is gamma = E[Z^3], the third standardized moment. Kurtosis is kappa = E[Z^4], the fourth, with no subtraction of 3 in this lesson (Definition 2.2).

front: How are skewness and kurtosis written in central moments?
back: Hypotheses: at least two values, positive weights. gamma = m_3/sigma^3, kappa = m_4/sigma^4 = m_4/m_2^2, E[Z] = 0 and E[Z^2] = 1 (Proposition 2.2).

front: How do skewness and kurtosis change under Y = aX + b with a not zero?
back: Kurtosis is unchanged, and skewness is multiplied by sign(a) (Proposition 2.3).

front: What is the lower bound on kurtosis, and when is it attained?
back: Hypotheses: at least two values, positive weights. kappa >= 1, with equality if and only if X takes exactly two values, each with probability 1/2 (Proposition 2.4).

front: What are the skewness and kurtosis of a Bernoulli law with P(X = 1) = p?
back: With q = 1 - p and 0 < p < 1: gamma = (1 - 2p)/sqrt(pq) and kappa = (1 - 3pq)/(pq) (Example 2.5).

front: What are the central moments of the law on 0, 1, 2, 10 with probabilities 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/8?
What is the kurtosis of the law on -2, 1, 3 with probabilities 2/5, 1/2, 1/10?
back: 5/3, from mean 0, m_2 = 3 and m_4 = 15 (Section 4).

front: Does a skewness of zero mean the law is symmetric?
back: No. The law on -2, 1, 3 with probabilities 2/5, 1/2, 1/10 has gamma = 0 and is not symmetric about its mean (Section 4).

front: Is the kurtosis of every law equal to 3?
back: No. The Bernoulli law with p = 1/10 has kappa = 73/9, and p = 1/4 gives kappa = 7/3 (Example 2.5).

front: Does reversing the sign of X leave its skewness unchanged?
back: No. For Y = -X, gamma_Y = -gamma_X (Proposition 2.3 with a = -1). The kurtosis is unchanged.

front: What skewness and kurtosis does the seed-2026 sample of 20000 draws print?
back: Skewness 2.065 and kurtosis 5.580, against exact values 2.073 and 5.625 for the same law.

front: Do the Bernoulli closed forms of Lab 3 agree with the moment definitions at p = 1/10?
back: Yes. The squared skewness is 64/9 and the kurtosis is 73/9, and both agree exactly with the moment definitions (Lab 3 prints True for each).

front: What is a joint table and what are its marginals?
back: A list of values p(x,y) >= 0 over pairs of values with total 1. The marginals are P(X = x) = sum over y of p(x,y) and P(Y = y) = sum over x of p(x,y) (Definition 1.1).

front: When are two events independent?
back: When P(A and B) = P(A) P(B) (Definition 1.2).

front: When are discrete random variables X and Y independent?
back: When p(x,y) = P(X = x) P(Y = y) for every pair (x,y) of values, so every cell of the joint table is the product of its two marginals (Definition 1.2).

front: Is the independence test applied cell by cell?
back: Yes. One cell that fails the product rule makes the pair dependent (Remark 1.3).

front: Are two events with positive probability and no common outcome independent?
back: No. Their intersection has probability 0, while P(A) P(B) > 0, so they are dependent (Proposition 1.4).

front: What is E[XY] for independent variables with finitely many values?
back: E[XY] = E[X] E[Y] (Proposition 1.5).

front: What is the covariance of X and Y?
back: Cov(X,Y) = E[(X - E[X])(Y - E[Y])] (Definition 1.6).

front: What is the shortcut formula for covariance?
back: Hypothesis: finitely many values. Cov(X,Y) = E[XY] - E[X] E[Y] (Proposition 1.7).

front: Do independent variables with finitely many values have zero covariance?
back: Yes, Cov(X,Y) = 0 (Proposition 1.8). The converse is false (Example 1.9).

front: Does zero covariance imply independence?
back: No. For X uniform on {-1, 0, 1} and Y = X^2, the covariance is 0, but p(0,0) = 1/3 while P(X = 0) P(Y = 0) = 1/9 (Example 1.9).

front: What are the conditional distribution and the conditional expectation of X given Y = y, in the elementary form?
back: For P(Y = y) > 0: P(X = x | Y = y) = p(x,y)/P(Y = y), and E[X | Y = y] = sum over x of x P(X = x | Y = y) (Definition 2.1). Only finite tables are covered (Remark 2.2).

front: Does total expectation hold for a finite table?
back: Yes. E[X] = sum over y with P(Y = y) > 0 of E[X | Y = y] P(Y = y) (Proposition 2.3).

front: Under independence, does E[X | Y = y] equal E[X]?
back: Yes, for every y with P(Y = y) > 0 (Proposition 2.4).

front: What are the conditional expectations for the dependent table of Example 2.5?
back: E[X | Y = 0] = 1 with P(Y = 0) = 2/5, and E[X | Y = 1] = 2/3 with P(Y = 1) = 3/5. E[X] = 4/5, and the total-expectation sum is also 4/5 (Example 2.5; Lab 1 Part C).

front: What does Lab 1 Part B print for the covariance and the independence verdict of X and Y = X^2?
back: Covariance 0 with independent False; the cell (0,0) has joint probability 1/3 against the product 1/9 (Lab 1, Part B).

front: What does knowing that a disjoint event A occurred tell you about an event B of positive probability?
back: That B did not occur. Disjoint events with positive probability are dependent (Proposition 1.4).

front: Is E[X | Y = y] always the same as E[X]?
back: No. Equality holds under independence (Proposition 2.4). For the dependent table of Example 2.5, E[X | Y = 0] = 1 and E[X | Y = 1] = 2/3, while E[X] = 4/5.

front: What is the joint probability of cell (0,0) in the product table of Lab 1 Part A?
back: 3/50, the product of P(X = 0) = 1/5 and P(Y = 0) = 3/10. The lab prints the same value for the cell's product of marginals.

front: What is the standard deviation of X?
back: sigma_X = sqrt(Var(X)), the nonnegative square root of the variance (Definition 1.3).

front: What is the correlation of X and Y?
back: rho(X,Y) = Cov(X,Y)/(sigma_X sigma_Y), defined when both standard deviations are positive. A constant has no correlation (Definition 1.4).

front: Which algebraic properties does covariance have?
back: Hypothesis: finitely many values. Covariance is symmetric. Cov(aX + b, Y) = a Cov(X,Y), Cov(X + Z, Y) = Cov(X,Y) + Cov(Z,Y), and Cov(X,X) = Var(X) >= 0 (Proposition 1.1).

front: How does covariance scale?
back: Cov(aX + b, cY + d) = ac Cov(X,Y), and Var(aX + b) = a^2 Var(X) (Proposition 1.2).

front: What bound does Cauchy-Schwarz give for covariance and correlation?
back: Hypothesis: finitely many values. Cov(X,Y)^2 <= Var(X) Var(Y). So when both standard deviations are positive, -1 <= rho <= 1 (Proposition 1.5).

front: Is correlation unchanged by positive affine maps?
back: Yes, when sigma_X > 0 and sigma_Y > 0. For a, c > 0 and any b and d, rho(aX + b, cY + d) = rho(X,Y) (Proposition 1.6).

front: What is the correlation of X and Y = aX + b when a > 0 and sigma_X > 0?
back: 1 (Example 1.7): Cov(X,Y) = a Var(X) and sigma_Y = a sigma_X.

front: Can correlation be zero for a pair that is a function of X?
back: Yes. For X uniform on {-1, 0, 1} and Y = X^2, Cov(X,Y) = 0 and rho = 0, though Y is a function of X (Remark 1.8).

front: What is the covariance matrix of a vector X = (X_1, X_2 through X_n)?
back: The n by n matrix with entries Sigma_ij = Cov(X_i, X_j). Its diagonal entries are the variances (Definition 2.1).

front: What does it mean for a real symmetric matrix M to be positive semidefinite?
back: w^T M w >= 0 for every vector w (Definition 2.2).

front: Is every covariance matrix positive semidefinite?
back: Yes. A covariance matrix is symmetric, and w^T Sigma w = Var(sum of w_i X_i) >= 0 for every w (Proposition 2.3). The hypothesis is finitely many values.

front: What bounds hold for the entries of a covariance matrix?
back: Every diagonal entry is nonnegative, and Sigma_ij^2 <= Sigma_ii Sigma_jj for all i and j (Proposition 2.4).

front: Does zero correlation mean the two variables are unrelated?
back: No. Remark 1.8 gives Y = X^2 with X uniform on {-1, 0, 1}: the correlation is 0 while Y is a function of X. Correlation measures linear association.

front: Is covariance unit-free, like correlation?
back: No. Cov(100X, 100Y) = 10^4 Cov(X,Y) (Proposition 1.2), while the correlation is unchanged by the same scaling (Proposition 1.6).

front: Is any symmetric matrix with positive diagonal entries a covariance matrix?
back: No. The matrix [[1, 2], [2, 1]] is symmetric with positive diagonal, but it needs 2^2 <= 1 by Proposition 2.4, which is false.

front: What largest entry error does Lab 1 Part A print for the sample covariance matrix at n = 20000, against Sigma?
back: 0.00002223, against 0.00016257 at n = 100. The seeded sample is one run from the two-asset construction.

front: What sample correlation does the seeded run of Lab 1 Part B print at n = 20000, against rho = 0.6?
What is the normal distribution N(mu, sigma^2)?
back: The law with density exp(-(x - mu)^2/(2 sigma^2))/(sigma sqrt(2 pi)) on the real line, for sigma > 0. The standard normal density is phi(z) = e^(-z^2/2)/sqrt(2 pi) (Definition 1.1).

front: What is the value of the Gaussian integral?
back: The integral of e^(-x^2/2) over the real line equals sqrt(2 pi) (Proposition 1.2), proved by squaring the integral and changing to polar coordinates. Under Assumption 1.

front: Is the normal density a probability density?
back: Yes. For sigma > 0 and real mu, the density is nonnegative and integrates to 1 (Proposition 1.3). Under Assumption 1.

front: What does standardization give for a normal variable?
back: If X ~ N(mu, sigma^2) with sigma > 0, then (X - mu)/sigma has the law N(0,1). Conversely, if Z is standard normal, then mu + sigma Z has the law N(mu, sigma^2) (Proposition 1.4). Under Assumption 1.

front: What are the mean and the variance of N(mu, sigma^2)?
back: E[X] = mu and Var(X) = sigma^2. For the standard normal, E[Z] = 0 and E[Z^2] = 1 (Proposition 1.5; the second moment is found by integration by parts). Under Assumption 1.

front: What is a chi-square variable with nu degrees of freedom?
back: W_nu = Z_1^2 + Z_2^2 + through Z_nu^2 for independent standard normal Z_i, with nu a positive integer (Definition 2.1).

front: What Laplace-transform identity does Lemma 2.3 give for a squared normal?
back: For s >= 0, E[e^(-s Z^2)] = (1 + 2s)^(-1/2) for a standard normal Z. For a chi-square W with nu degrees of freedom, E[1/W] = the integral from 0 to infinity of (1 + 2s)^(-nu/2) ds (Lemma 2.3). Under Assumption 1.

front: What is E[1/W] for a chi-square variable W with nu degrees of freedom?
back: Hypothesis: nu a positive integer. If nu > 2, E[1/W] = 1/(nu - 2). If nu <= 2, E[1/W] is infinite (Proposition 2.4). Under Assumption 1.

front: What is the Student-t distribution with nu degrees of freedom?
back: The law of T = Z / sqrt(W/nu), with Z standard normal and W chi-square with nu degrees of freedom, independent of Z. The page treats positive integer nu only (Definition 2.5).

front: What are the mean and the variance of the Student-t?
back: Hypothesis: nu a positive integer. If nu > 2, E[T] = 0 and Var(T) = nu/(nu - 2). If nu <= 2, E[T^2] is infinite (Proposition 2.6). Under Assumption 1.

front: What is Var(T_5)?
back: 5/3, from nu/(nu - 2) with nu = 5 (Proposition 2.6). Under Assumption 1.

front: Does a Student-t variable have variance 1 because it is standardized?
back: No. A Student-t with nu > 2 degrees of freedom has mean 0 and variance nu/(nu - 2), not 1. For nu = 5 this is 5/3 (Proposition 2.6). Under Assumption 1.

front: Does every Student-t have a finite variance, as every normal does?
back: No. For nu <= 2, E[T^2] = nu E[1/W] is infinite (Proposition 2.6). Under Assumption 1.

front: Are the two parameters of N(mu, sigma^2) its mean and its variance?
back: Yes. N(mu, sigma^2) has mean mu and variance sigma^2 (Proposition 1.5). Under Assumption 1.

front: What sample variance of T at nu = 5 does Lab 1 Part A print, against 5/3?
back: 1.669114 against the formula 1.666667. The relative error 0.001469 is computed from unrounded values (n = 100000 seeded draws).

front: What is the moment-generating function of X, and what is its domain?
back: M_X(t) = E[e^(tX)] for each real t where this expectation is finite. The domain is the set of such t and always contains 0, where M_X(0) = 1 (Definition 1.1).

front: Is the moment-generating function of a finitely valued X finite for every real t?
back: Yes. Its domain is the whole real line (Proposition 1.2).

front: What is the moment-generating function of N(mu, sigma^2)?
back: exp(mu t + sigma^2 t^2/2) for every real t (Proposition 1.3), proved by completing the square. Under Assumption 1.

front: What is the moment-generating function of the square of a standard normal?
back: E[e^(tZ^2)] = (1 - 2t)^(-1/2) for t < 1/2, and it is infinite for t >= 1/2. The domain is (-infinity, 1/2) (Proposition 1.4). Under Assumption 1.

front: What is the complex exponential e^(ia)?
back: cos a + i sin a, with modulus 1 (Definition 2.1).

front: What is the characteristic function of X?
back: phi_X(t) = E[e^(itX)] for each real t (Definition 2.2).

front: Does the characteristic function always exist, and what bounds it?
back: Hypothesis: X has finitely many values or has a density. Then phi_X(t) exists for every real t, |phi_X(t)| <= 1, and phi_X(0) = 1 (Proposition 2.3).

front: How does the characteristic function transform under Y = aX + b?
back: phi_(aX+b)(t) = e^(itb) phi_X(at) for every real t (Proposition 2.4).

front: What is the characteristic function of a two-point law with P(X = a) = p and P(X = b) = 1 - p?
back: phi_X(t) = p e^(ita) + (1 - p) e^(itb), and |phi_X(t)|^2 = p^2 + (1 - p)^2 + 2p(1 - p) cos(t(a - b)) (Proposition 2.5).

front: What is the moment-generating function of a sum of independent finitely valued variables?
back: Hypothesis: X and Y independent with finitely many values. M_(X+Y)(t) = M_X(t) M_Y(t) for every real t (Problem P3; proof in Section 5, which uses independence).

front: Is the moment-generating function of every random variable finite for every real t?
back: No. For W = Z^2, E[e^(tW)] is infinite for t >= 1/2 (Proposition 1.4). Under Assumption 1.

front: Is the moment-generating function of a sum the sum of the two functions?
back: No. For independent variables with finitely many values the rule is the product, M_(X+Y) = M_X M_Y. If X = Y, then M_(X+Y)(t) = M_X(2t).

front: Does the characteristic function exist only for a variable with a density?
back: No. It exists for every finitely valued variable (Proposition 2.3), and the two-point law of Proposition 2.5 has no density.

front: What is the largest absolute difference between Simpson's rule and the closed-form normal MGF in Lab 1 Part A?
back: 7.11e-13, at t = 2, where the closed form is 244.69193226. This is a numerical check, not a simulation.

front: What is the seeded sample mean of cos(X) at t = 1 in Lab 1 Part C, against the real part of phi(1)?
back: -0.062124, against -0.062110 for the real part of phi(1).

front: What is a standard normal vector of length k?
back: A vector Z = (Z_1, Z_2 through Z_k) whose coordinates are independent, each with the standard normal law of Lesson 6.

front: What are the second moments of a standard normal vector?
back: E[Z_i Z_j] = 1 if i = j and 0 if i is not j. In matrix form E[ZZ^T] = I (Proposition 1.1).

front: When is a random vector X multivariate normal with mean mu and covariance matrix Sigma?
back: When X has the same law as mu + AZ for some matrix A with AA^T = Sigma, where Z is a standard normal vector. A is a factor of Sigma (Definition 1.2).

front: What are the mean and covariance matrix of X = mu + AZ?
back: E[X] = mu, and the covariance matrix is AA^T (Proposition 1.3).

front: Is the factor of a covariance matrix unique?
back: No. If QQ^T = I, then AQ is also a factor of AA^T and gives the same mean and covariance (Remark 1.4).

front: For A = [[2, 0], [1, 1]] and mu = (1, -2), what are AA^T and A^T A?
back: AA^T = [[4, 2], [2, 2]], which is Sigma. A^T A = [[5, 1], [1, 1]], which is a different matrix. The factor B = AQ = [[0, -2], [1, -1]] also gives BB^T = Sigma (Example 1.5).

front: Is AA^T symmetric and nonnegative in the quadratic form sense?
back: Yes. (AA^T)^T = AA^T, and w^T AA^T w = |A^T w|^2 >= 0 for every w (Proposition 1.6).

front: Does a singular covariance matrix have an inverse?
back: No. If Sigma = AA^T is not positive definite, some nonzero w has Sigma w = 0, so Sigma has no inverse (Proposition 2.1).

front: Do normal margins fix the joint law?
back: No. X and Y = epsilon X are standard normal and uncorrelated, yet P(X + Y = 0) >= 1/2, while X and an independent standard normal X' have P(X + X' = 0) = 0 (Section 4).

front: Is a vector whose coordinates are each normal multivariate normal?
back: Not by that fact alone. Normal coordinates say nothing about the joint law (Section 4). Definition 1.2 concerns the whole vector and needs the factor A of the whole vector.

front: Is the covariance of AZ equal to A^T A?
back: No. The covariance of AZ is AA^T (Proposition 1.3). Example 1.5 computes both products for the same A, and they differ.

front: Is the matrix of Example 1.5 positive definite?
back: Yes. For Sigma = [[4, 2], [2, 2]], w^T Sigma w = (2w_1 + w_2)^2 + w_2^2, which is zero only when w = 0 (Example 1.5).

front: What is the largest entry gap, from Sigma, of the seed-2026 sample covariance of X in Lab 1 Part B?
back: 0.0187, in the off-diagonal entries (n = 20000, one run).
basis: Lab 1, Part B (SIMULATED; seed 2026; n = 20000; one run)

front: What is Chebyshev's inequality?
back: Hypothesis: a finitely valued Y with mean m and variance v, and a > 0. Then P(|Y - m| >= a) <= v/a^2 (Proposition 1.1).

front: What are the mean and the variance of the sample mean?
back: Hypotheses: identically distributed X_i with mean mu and variance sigma^2, where 0 < sigma^2 < infinity, and X_i and X_j independent for i not equal to j. Then E[Xbar_n] = mu and Var(Xbar_n) = sigma^2/n (Proposition 1.2).

front: What does the weak law of large numbers state in this lesson?
back: Hypotheses: identically distributed X_i with mean mu and variance sigma^2, where 0 < sigma^2 < infinity, X_i and X_j independent for i not equal to j, and every law finitely valued. Then P(|Xbar_n - mu| >= eps) <= sigma^2/(n eps^2) for every eps > 0 and every n >= 1, so the probability tends to 0 (Theorem 1.3).

front: What does the law of large numbers mean in this lesson?
back: For identically distributed variables with mean mu, P(|Xbar_n - mu| >= eps) tends to 0 as n grows, for every eps > 0 (Definition 1.4).

front: Which dependence hypothesis does the weak law's proof use?
back: Only pairwise independence, through the zero covariance E[(X_i - mu)(X_j - mu)] = 0 for i not equal to j (Proposition 1.2 and the text after Theorem 1.3).

front: What is the product rule for independent variables and their characteristic functions?
back: Hypothesis: X_1, X_2 through X_n independent. E[prod g_i(X_i)] = prod E[g_i(X_i)], so phi of the sum is the product of the phi_(X_i). For i.i.d. variables the product is phi_X(t)^n (Proposition 2.1).

front: What is the expansion of a characteristic function near zero?
back: Hypotheses: Y finitely valued with E[Y] = 0, E[Y^2] = 1, M = max|Y| > 0, and |s| <= 1/M. Then |phi_Y(s) - (1 - s^2/2)| <= |s|^3 E|Y|^3/3 (Proposition 2.2).

front: What does Proposition 2.3 prove about the standardized sample mean Z_n?
back: Under the i.i.d. hypotheses: (a) E[Z_n] = 0 and E[Z_n^2] = 1 for every n; (b) phi_(Z_n)(t) tends to e^(-t^2/2) for every real t (Proposition 2.3).

front: Is the central limit theorem's conclusion about distribution functions proved on the page?
back: No. Proposition 2.3(b) is proved, but the distribution-function conclusion needs two further steps: (i) that e^(-t^2/2) is the characteristic function of the standard normal law, and (ii) convergence of distribution functions from characteristic functions. The page establishes neither (Section 2; Problem R2).

front: What is the central limit theorem in the sense of this lesson?
back: The CLT holds for X when P(Z_n <= z) tends to Phi(z) for every real z, where Phi is the standard normal distribution function (Definition 2.4).

front: Can the sample mean of a finitely valued law have a normal distribution for some n?
back: No. Its distribution function jumps, while a normal law has a density and no jumps (Section 3).

front: Does the law of large numbers say the sample mean is close to mu at every n?
back: No. Theorem 1.3 bounds the probability of a large deviation at each n, and that bound tends to 0 only as n grows.

front: Does the central limit theorem mean the sample mean is normally distributed for large n?
back: No. The theorem concerns the standardized mean Z_n and its limit (Definition 2.4). A finitely valued sample mean has no normal law for any finite n (Section 3).

front: Does the central limit theorem need the variables themselves to be normal?
back: No. The statement needs i.i.d. copies with finitely many values and variance sigma^2 > 0 (Section 2). The die of Lab 1 is not normal. Proposition 2.3(b) gives the limit e^(-t^2/2) of the characteristic functions without assuming normality, and the step to distribution functions is not proved on the page.

front: What is the Chebyshev bound on P(|Xbar_100 - 3.5| >= 0.5) for the fair die?
back: 7/60, about 0.1167, from sigma^2/(n eps^2) with sigma^2 = 35/12 (Problem M1).

front: What exact probability does Lab 1 Part A give for P(Z_10 <= 1), and what is its gap to Phi(1)?
back: 0.843496 from P(S_10 <= 40), with gap +0.002151 to Phi(1) = 0.841345. The threshold is 40 because 35 + sqrt(29.1667) = 40.4006 (Problem E1).

front: What estimate does Lab 1 Part C give for P(Z_5 <= 1), and what standard error does it print?
back: 0.8552, with standard error 0.0056, from 4000 seeded replications.
basis: Lab 1, Part C (SIMULATED; seed 2026; 4000 replications at n = 5)

front: What is a heavy-tailed random variable?
back: X is heavy-tailed when e^(cx) P(|X| > x) tends to infinity as x grows, for every c > 0 (Definition 1.1). A law that is not heavy-tailed is light-tailed in this lesson.

front: What are the standard Cauchy law and the Student-t law with 3 degrees of freedom?
back: The standard Cauchy density is 1/(pi(1 + x^2)). The t(3) density is 2/(pi sqrt 3)(1 + t^2/3)^(-2), the law of Lesson 6 at nu = 3, taken as Assumption 1 (Definition 1.2).

front: What is the distribution function of the standard Cauchy law?
back: F_C(x) = 1/2 + (1/pi) arctan x (Proposition 1.3).

front: What is the distribution function of the t(3) law?
back: F_V(x) = 1/2 + (1/pi)(arctan(x/sqrt 3) + (x/sqrt 3)/(1 + x^2/3)) (Proposition 1.3). Under Assumption 1.

front: What is P(|C| > x) for the standard Cauchy law and x > 0?
back: (2/pi) arctan(1/x) (Proposition 1.4).

front: What is P(|V| > x) for the t(3) law and x > 0?
back: (2/pi)(arctan(sqrt 3/x) - x sqrt 3/(3 + x^2)) (Proposition 1.4). Under Assumption 1.

front: Are the Cauchy and t(3) laws heavy-tailed, and is the standard normal?
back: The Cauchy and t(3) laws are heavy-tailed. The standard normal is light-tailed, since P(|Z| > x) <= 2 e^(-x^2/2) for x > 0 (Proposition 1.5). Under Assumption 1.

front: What are the limits of the scaled tails?
back: As x grows, x P(|C| > x) tends to 2/pi, and x^3 P(|V| > x) tends to 4 sqrt 3/pi (Proposition 1.7). Under Assumption 1.

front: Does the standard Cauchy law have a mean or a finite variance?
back: No. E|C| and E[C^2] are both infinite, so E[C] is not defined and the variance is not finite (Proposition 2.1).

front: What is the variance of the t(3) law?
back: 3, cited from Lesson 6 as nu/(nu - 2) at nu = 3. The lesson does not derive it (Remark 2.2).

front: Is the fourth moment of the t(3) law finite?
back: No. E[V^4] is infinite, so the kurtosis of Lesson 3 is not defined for V (Proposition 2.3). Under Assumption 1.

front: What is the failure of the CLT under infinite variance?
back: The situation in which Var(X) is not finite. The standardization of Lesson 9 then has no finite sigma, so the normal limit is not available for it (Definition 2.4).

front: Does the page prove that the sample mean of standard Cauchy copies is standard Cauchy for every n?
back: No. Remark 2.5 states it without proof, without a citation and without a grade.

front: Does a heavy tail mean large values occur often?
back: Not by itself. A heavy tail describes the decay of P(|X| > x) as x grows (Definition 1.1), not the size of one tail probability. For the Cauchy law at x = 10, P(|C| > 10) = (2/pi) arctan(0.1) = 0.063451, about 1 draw in 16, against 1.5240 x 10^-23 for the normal.

front: Does averaging always reduce the spread of a sample mean by the factor sqrt(n)?
back: No. The sqrt(n) scaling is Lesson 9's result for finite variance, and the Cauchy law has no finite variance (Proposition 2.1). The standard Cauchy interquartile range of one draw is 2 (Problem P2).

front: Does the Cauchy law have mean 0 by symmetry, so that the sample mean estimates 0?
back: No. Symmetry does not give a mean when the integral does not converge absolutely. E|C| is infinite (Proposition 2.1), so E[C] is not defined.

front: What are the quartiles of the standard Cauchy law, and what is their difference?
back: -1 and 1, from F_C(q) = 1/4 and 3/4, so the interquartile range is 2 (Problem P2).

front: What does x P(|C| > x) equal at x = 10 in Lab 1 Part D, and how does it compare with 2/pi?
back: 0.634510, from (2/pi) arctan(0.1) times 10. The limit is 2/pi, about 0.636620, so the value at x = 10 is about 0.002 below it (Problem E1).

front: What interquartile ranges of the Cauchy sample mean does Lab 1 Part C print at n = 10 and n = 100?
back: 1.8220 at n = 10 and 1.8838 at n = 100, from 400 seeded replications. The exact range of one draw is 2.
basis: Lab 1, Part C (SIMULATED; 400 seeded replications per size)

front: Are the results of Lab 1 theorems on this page?
back: No. They are simulation output and one-seed paths, and the lab does not establish the limit it prints. Only the statements graded T are proved on the page.

front: Does the page state a density formula for the multivariate normal law?
back: No. No density is stated, derived or used on this page (Section 2).

back: 0.833333, 0.847994, 0.843496, 0.835793 and 0.833926, from the die's exact mass function (Lab 1, Part A).

back: 2.205308, against the limit 4 sqrt(3)/pi, about 2.2053 (Proposition 1.7). Under Assumption 1.

front: What is the infimum of a set A of real numbers that is bounded below?
back: inf A is the greatest real number that is at most every member of A (Section 3).

front: When are variables X and Y independent in Remark 2.2?
back: When P(X in A, Y in B) = P(X in A) P(Y in B) for all sets A and B (Remark 2.2).

front: When is a symmetric matrix M positive definite?
back: When w^T M w > 0 for every nonzero vector w (Section 1, after Proposition 1.6).

front: What is the sample covariance matrix with divisor n - 1?
back: For draws X^(1) to X^(n) of a random vector, its (r, s) entry is the sum over t of (X_r^(t) - Xbar_r)(X_s^(t) - Xbar_s), divided by n - 1, where Xbar_r is the sample mean of coordinate r (Section 3).

front: What does it mean for the variables of the sample mean to be identically distributed?
back: Each X_i has the same law as a fixed X, with mean mu and variance sigma^2, where 0 < sigma^2 < infinity (Section 1).

front: What is the sample mean Xbar_n of the first n variables?
back: The sum of the first n variables divided by n (Section 1).

front: What does i.i.d. mean for the variables of Section 2?
back: Independent and identically distributed: the joint probability of any tuple of values factorizes into the product of the one-variable probabilities, and each X_i has the law of X (Section 2).

front: What is a light-tailed law in this lesson?
back: A law that is not heavy-tailed (Section 1, after Definition 1.1).
